## Section 1 code:

```{r section1-code, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# Not run when knitting (it reads the 130 MB raw file). Set eval = TRUE to rebuild data/daily.csv.


load_minutes <- function(path) {
  df <- read.csv(
    path, sep = ";", na.strings = "?", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    colClasses = c("character", "character", "numeric", "NULL", "NULL", "NULL",
                   "numeric", "numeric", "numeric")
  )
  names(df) <- c("Date", "Time", "Global_active_power", "Sub_metering_1", "Sub_metering_2", "Sub_metering_3")
  df$date <- as.Date(df$Date, format = "%d/%m/%Y")
  df
}

#group minutes by date and aggregates to days
aggregate_daily <- function(df) {
  g <- as.integer(df$date)
  zero_na <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), 0, x)
  n_obs <- rowsum(as.numeric(!is.na(df$Global_active_power)), g, reorder = TRUE)
  kwh_raw <- rowsum(zero_na(df$Global_active_power), g, reorder = TRUE) / 60
  sub_kwh <- rowsum(
    zero_na(df$Sub_metering_1) + zero_na(df$Sub_metering_2) + zero_na(df$Sub_metering_3),
    g, reorder = TRUE
  ) / 1000
  n_rows <- rowsum(rep(1, nrow(df)), g, reorder = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    date = as.Date(as.integer(rownames(n_obs)), origin = "1970-01-01"),
    n_obs = as.numeric(n_obs), # number of minutes that have a power reading
    kwh_raw = as.numeric(kwh_raw), # sum of power/60 (will be used later)
    sub_kwh = as.numeric(sub_kwh),
    n_rows = as.numeric(n_rows), # how many minute rows the day has (to check that every day has 1440 rows later)
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

main <- function() {
  # ROOT <- script_root()
  # RAW <- file.path(ROOT, "data", "household_power_consumption.txt")
  RAW <- here("data", "household_power_consumption.txt")
  
  MIN_COVERAGE <- 0.95 # 95% rule
  MINUTES_PER_DAY <- 1440
  # for (sub in c("figures", "results")) dir.create(file.path(ROOT, sub), showWarnings = FALSE)

  cat("reading raw file ...\n")
  minutes <- load_minutes(RAW)
  n_rows <- nrow(minutes)
  n_missing <- sum(is.na(minutes$Global_active_power))
  daily <- aggregate_daily(minutes)
  # Time used to verify one row per minute (no repeated time stamps)
  stopifnot(!any(duplicated(minutes[, c("Date", "Time")])))
  rm(minutes) # everything is on a daily scale now

  # first <- daily$date[1]
  # last <- daily$date[nrow(daily)]
  daily <- daily[-c(1, nrow(daily)), ] # removed partial first and last days
  # every day should have all 1,440 minute rows (timestamps), even if some readings are "?"
  stopifnot(all(daily$n_rows == 1440))
  #build the full calendar and apply the 95% rule
  full_dates <- seq(min(daily$date), max(daily$date), by = "day")
  full <- merge(data.frame(date = full_dates), daily, by = "date", all.x = TRUE, sort = TRUE)
  stopifnot(nrow(full) == nrow(daily))  # no calendar day is absent from the raw file
  full$n_obs[is.na(full$n_obs)] <- 0 # ensure missing days don't have NA, but have 0 instead to indicate no recordings
  # coverage = minutes with a power reading / 1440; days below 95% are labelled missing
  full$coverage <- full$n_obs / MINUTES_PER_DAY
  # full$coverage[is.na(full$coverage)] <- 0
  full$observed <- full$coverage >= MIN_COVERAGE # mark the days with 95% coverage
  #for retained days with few missing values, re-scale the daily total 
  # (equivalent to filling each missing minute on a retained day with that day's 
  #  average observed power then summing all 1440 minutes to get daily energy)
  full$kwh <- ifelse(full$observed, full$kwh_raw * MINUTES_PER_DAY / full$n_obs, NA_real_) # our final response var (Y_d)
  full$t <- seq_len(nrow(full)) # day counter (1:1440) for use in harmonics
  full$dow <- as.integer(format(full$date, "%u")) - 1L # day of week (0=Monday,..., 6=Sunday)
  full$year <- as.integer(format(full$date, "%Y")) 
  full$doy <- as.integer(format(full$date, "%j"))

  obs <- full[full$observed, ]
  bad <- sum(obs$sub_kwh > obs$kwh_raw, na.rm = TRUE) # verify that sub-meters < total

  out <- full[, c("date", "t", "kwh", "dow", "n_obs", "coverage", "observed", "sub_kwh", "year", "doy")]
  op <- options(digits = 15, scipen = 999)
  on.exit(options(op), add = TRUE)
  write.csv(out, here("data", "daily.csv"), row.names = FALSE, na = "")

  cat(sprintf("minutes: %d, missing power: %d (%.2f%%)\n", n_rows, n_missing, 100 * n_missing / n_rows))
  cat(sprintf("calendar days: %d, retained: %d, missing: %d (no data at all: %d)\n",
              nrow(full), sum(full$observed), sum(!full$observed), sum(full$n_obs == 0)))
  cat(sprintf("sub-meters > total on retained days: %d (expect 0)\n", bad))
  }

main()
```

# 1. Introduction

Residential electricity demand varies over time because of household activity, weekly patterns, seasonal changes, holidays, and many other factors. Accurately forecasting electricity demand is crucial for energy planning and management. The objective of this project is to characterize temporal patterns in daily household electricity consumption and develop a Bayesian analysis that can be used to predict future daily electricity demand, as well as quantify uncertainty in those predictions. Further, a non-Bayesian alternative approach is to be considered and compared with the Bayesian model. To do so, we utilize the UCI *Individual Household Electric Power Consumption* dataset.

## 1.1 Scientific Questions and the Model

Through exploratory data analysis and our building of our Bayesian model, we will attempt to answer the following:

1.  How does daily household electricity consumption vary over the study period?

2.  Is there evidence of a long-term increase or decrease in electricity consumption?

3.  What annual seasonal pattern is present, and does the second harmonic provide an important improvement over the first-harmonic representation?

4.  Are there systematic weekly patterns in electricity demand?

5.  How accurate can future daily electricity consumption be predicted, and how does predictive uncertainty change with the forecasting horizon?

6.  Are there periods of unusually high or low electricity consumption that are not adequately explained by the fitted model?

## 1.2 Why Is This a Bayesian Problem

These scientific questions don't necessarily have to be answered with a Bayesian model. Using frequentist techniques, we can answer all these questions by simply fitting a harmonic regression with AR errors, estimating parameters, constructing prediction intervals, and then forecasting future electricity consumption. However, using Bayesian methods, we can better quantify uncertainty that's occurring at all levels of the data (unknown seasonal effects, unknown AR dependence, unknown tail behavior, missing observations, etc.), as well as propagate that uncertainty in all our forecasts. For example, we could have a posterior distribution for every quantity and predictive distribution for every future day. This is why we'd utilize a Bayesian model specifically.

## 1.3 The Data

### 1.3.1 Overall Data Structure

The UCI *Individual Household Electric Power Consumption* dataset records 2,075,259 one-minute electric power consumption measurements from a single house (not a grid) in Sceaux, France between December 2006 and November 2010 (47 months). Each instance contains nine recorded variables: `Date`, `Time`, `Global_active_power`,`Global_reactive_power`, `Voltage`, `Global_intensity`,`Sub_metering_1`,`Sub_metering_2`,and `Sub_metering_3`.

Of the nine recorded variables in the dataset, only `Global_active_power` enters the analysis after being transformed into daily energy. `Time` is used in data cleaning to verify every full day contains exactly 1440 unique minutes. `Date` is retained to construct the temporal predictors, a linear trend, annual sine/cosine harmonics (period 365), and day-of-week indicators. The remaining electrical channels are discarded since`Global_reactive_power` and `Voltage` are irrelevant to active energy consumption, and `Global_intensity` is nearly collinear with `Global_active_power`. The three sub-metering channels are retained solely as a consistency check, since they do not sum to the whole-house total.

### 1.3.2 Data Cleaning


Missing readings are coded as `?` in the raw file and dates are recorded day-first. Of the 2,075,259 minutes, 25,979 (1.25%) lack a power reading. We dropped the first and last days of the dataset as they have partial measurements and verified that every remaining day has 1,440 minute rows with no duplicate time stamps. For each day we computed $\text{Coverage} = \text{observed minutes} / 1440$ and labeled days with $\text{Coverage} \geq 0.95$ as *observed*. For the observed days that had missing minutes, we filled each missing minute with that day's average power (the equivalent of scaling up the day's total to 1,440 minutes). Days below the threshold were kept on the calendar but treated as *missing* rather than deleted, so the daily series remains a sequence of consecutive days. Low-consumption periods ("absence blocks") are fully recorded, so they are not treated as missing days. In the end, we have 1417 observed days and 23 missing days (9 with no readings at all and 14 with coverage of readings below 95%).

As a consistency check, we verified that the sub-meter energy never exceeded the house total on any observed day.

### 1.3.3 Data Transformation

The dataset provides `Global_active_power` (GAP), the household global minute-averaged active power in kilowatts (kW). The main objective is framed around daily energy consumption, so a transformation of this variable is essential. **Power (kW)** represents instantaneous rate of delivering energy and total **energy (kWh)** consumption over a time interval is obtained by summing discrete power values multiplied by the duration of each sampling interval (*Hébrail and Bérard, UCI Machine Learning Repository*).

In this dataset, each GAP value represents one minute of average power, and $1\text{ minute} = (1/60) \text{ hour}$. Thus, energy consumption in minute $m$ is $$E_m = \text{GAP}_m* \dfrac{1}{60} \text{ (kWh)}.$$

The daily total energy consumption is the sum over all 1440 minutes of day $d$ (because missing minutes were filled in Data Cleaning): $$\begin{aligned}
Y_d &= \sum_{m=1}^{1440} E_m \\[6pt]
&= \sum_{m=1}^{1440} \left( \text{GAP}_m * \frac{1}{60} \right) \\[6pt]
&= \frac{1}{60} \sum_{m=1}^{1440} \text{GAP}_m
\end{aligned}$$

$Y_d$ is computed only for days retained under our 0.95 coverage rule, and other days are treated as missing. $Y_d$ denotes the daily household energy consumption (kWh) and serves as our primary response variable for all subsequent analyses.

For the analysis, `daily.csv` is used. It contains the response variable $Y_d$ and other columns that were created based on the original dataset. The new columns are: `t`, `dow`, `n_obs`, `coverage`, `observed`, `sub_kwh`, `year`, `doy`. These new columns are essential for the model. (To rebuild `data/daily.csv`, download the UCI file into `data/` and set `eval = TRUE` in the Section 1 code chunk and run it.)

ORIGIN <- as.Date("2006-12-17")   # t = 1
MONTHS <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")
DOW_NAMES <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
MIN_COVERAGE <- 0.95              # 95% retention rule used in 01_aggregate.R (for Figure 1b)

library(here)   # install.packages("here") once; project root = folder containing .here

# [HELPERS] used by Figure 1
read_daily <- function(path) {
  d <- read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  d$date <- as.Date(d$date)
  d$observed <- tolower(as.character(d$observed)) %in% c("true", "t", "1")
  d
}

ols <- function(X, y) {
  beta <- qr.solve(X, y)
  list(beta = beta, resid = as.numeric(y - X %*% beta))
}

clim_day <- function(dates) {
  dates <- as.Date(dates)
  doy <- as.integer(format(dates, "%j"))
  y <- as.integer(format(dates, "%Y"))
  m <- as.integer(format(dates, "%m"))
  day <- as.integer(format(dates, "%d"))
  leap <- (y %% 4 == 0 & (y %% 100 != 0 | y %% 400 == 0))
  d <- as.numeric(doy)
  d[leap & m > 2] <- d[leap & m > 2] - 1
  d[m == 2 & day == 29] <- NA_real_
  d
}

smooth_on_clim <- function(clim, values, window = 15, circular = TRUE, min_frac = 0.6) {
  half <- window %/% 2
  s <- numeric(365)
  cnt <- numeric(365)
  for (i in seq_along(clim)) {
    if (is.na(clim[i]) || is.na(values[i])) next
    s[as.integer(clim[i])] <- s[as.integer(clim[i])] + values[i]
    cnt[as.integer(clim[i])] <- cnt[as.integer(clim[i])] + 1
  }
  out <- rep(NA_real_, 365)
  for (i in 0:364) {
    if (circular) idx <- ((i + (-half:half)) %% 365) + 1L
    else {
      ks <- (-half:half)
      ks <- ks[i + ks >= 0 & i + ks < 365]
      idx <- i + ks + 1L
    }
    cc <- sum(cnt[idx])
    if (cc >= window * min_frac) out[i + 1L] <- sum(s[idx]) / cc
  }
  out
}

dow_dummies <- function(dow, drop = 0) {
  levels <- setdiff(0:6, drop)
  out <- vapply(levels, function(k) as.numeric(dow == k), numeric(length(dow)))
  if (is.null(dim(out))) out <- matrix(out, ncol = 1)
  list(X = out, levels = levels)
}

harmonic_cols <- function(t, J) {
  if (J <= 0) return(matrix(0, length(t), 0))
  cols <- vector("list", 2 * J)
  k <- 1L
  for (j in seq_len(J)) {
    w <- 2 * pi * j * t / 365
    cols[[k]] <- sin(w); k <- k + 1L
    cols[[k]] <- cos(w); k <- k + 1L
  }
  do.call(cbind, cols)
}

harmonic_on_dates <- function(beta_harm, dates, J) {
  tt <- as.numeric(as.Date(dates) - ORIGIN) + 1
  h <- numeric(length(dates))
  for (j in seq_len(J)) {
    w <- 2 * pi * j * tt / 365
    h <- h + beta_harm[2 * j - 1] * sin(w) + beta_harm[2 * j] * cos(w)
  }
  h
}

# [DATA] read the cleaned daily series and set up the variables
dir.create(here("R_figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)

d <- read_daily(here("data", "daily.csv")) # all data (1440 days)
obs <- d[d$observed, ]
rownames(obs) <- NULL

y <- as.numeric(obs$kwh) # y = 1417 observed days
t <- as.numeric(obs$t)
dow <- as.integer(obs$dow)
month <- as.integer(format(obs$date, "%m"))
year <- as.integer(obs$year)
Dd <- dow_dummies(dow, 0)$X

# harmonic shape (for Fig 1c)
ref_dates <- seq(as.Date("2009-01-01"), as.Date("2009-12-31"), by = "day")
curves <- list()
for (J in 1:2) {
  fitJ <- ols(cbind(1, t / 365, harmonic_cols(t, J), Dd), y) # only observed days used
  harm <- fitJ$beta[3:(2 + 2 * J)]
  raw_curve <- harmonic_on_dates(harm, ref_dates, J)
  curve_J <- raw_curve - mean(raw_curve) + mean(y[year %in% 2007:2009])
  curves[[J]] <- curve_J
}
month_means <- vapply(1:12, function(m) mean(y[month == m]), numeric(1))

smooths <- lapply(names(year_colors), function(yr) {

})

# ---- Section 2.2 data setup ----
d <- read.csv(here("data", "daily.csv")) 
d$date <- as.Date(d$date)
# y redefined to be ALL 1440 days (not just the obsrved)
y  <- d$kwh # NA on missing days is fine
X  <- cbind(tc = (d$t - mean(d$t)) / 365,
            s1 = sin(2*pi*d$t/365), c1 = cos(2*pi*d$t/365),
            s2 = sin(4*pi*d$t/365), c2 = cos(4*pi*d$t/365),
            model.matrix(~ factor(d$dow))[, -1]) # 6 weekday dummies; arima adds the intercept

# Absence blocks: runs of >= 5 consecutive observed days below 12 kWh (EDA rule)
low <- !is.na(d$kwh) & d$kwh < 12
r <- rle(low)
ends <- cumsum(r$lengths) 
starts <- ends - r$lengths + 1
idx <- which(r$values & r$lengths >= 5)
blocks <- lapply(idx, function(i) as.character(d$date[c(starts[i], ends[i])]))
#blocks   # should list the same 4 blocks


# ---- Table 1 ----
# ACF of OLS residuals (trend + two harmonics + day of week), no AR term yet
# Shows the day-to-day correlation (to decide on AR(1) errors)

# OLS residuals (least squares): extreme days such as absence blocks get full weight
# and can inflate the autocorrelation

acf_row <- function(l, lags = c(1, 2, 3, 7)) {
  z <- if (l == 0) log(d$kwh) else (d$kwh^l - 1) / l   # Box-Cox transform (l = 0 is log)
  r <- residuals(lm(z ~ X, na.action = na.exclude)) # keeps NA on missing days, so lags line up
  a <- acf(r, lag.max = max(lags), na.action = na.pass, plot = FALSE)$acf[lags + 1]
  setNames(a, paste("Lag", lags))
}
acf_scales <- c("Log (λ = 0)" = 0, "Square root (λ = 0.5)" = 0.5, "kWh, no transform (λ = 1)" = 1)
acf_tab <- t(sapply(acf_scales, acf_row))

n_obs <- sum(!is.na(d$kwh))
tab1_kbl <- knitr::kable(round(acf_tab, 2),
             caption = paste0("Table 1. Autocorrelation of OLS residuals (trend + two harmonics + ",
                              "day of week) on each scale. Values beyond ±", round(1.96 / sqrt(n_obs), 2),
                              " differ from zero at the 5% level."))

# ---- Box-Cox profile likelihood ----
# Box-Cox that allows AR(1) errors 
# 1) WITH absence blocks:
# assumes normal innovations, so the heavy tails can pull λ around
y  <- d$kwh # NA on missing days is fine
X  <- cbind(tc = (d$t - mean(d$t)) / 365,
            s1 = sin(2*pi*d$t/365), c1 = cos(2*pi*d$t/365),
            s2 = sin(4*pi*d$t/365), c2 = cos(4*pi*d$t/365),
            model.matrix(~ factor(d$dow))[, -1]) # 6 weekday dummies; arima adds the intercept
lams <- seq(-0.5, 1.5, by = 0.1)
ll <- sapply(lams, function(l) {
  z <- if (l == 0) log(y) else (y^l - 1) / l
  fit <- arima(z, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
  fit$loglik + (l - 1) * sum(log(y), na.rm = TRUE)   # Jacobian, so scales are comparable
})
lams[which.max(ll)]
#plot(lams, ll, type = "b", xlab = "lambda", ylab = "profile log-likelihood")


# 2) WITHOUT absence blocks
#Mark the absence-block days
core <- rep(FALSE, nrow(d))
for (b in blocks) core[d$date >= as.Date(b[1]) & d$date <= as.Date(b[2])] <- TRUE
sum(core) # 57
# Copy y and blank out absence-block days
y_ex <- d$kwh
y_ex[core] <- NA
#profile likelihood on y_ex
ll_ex <- sapply(lams, function(l) {
  z <- if (l == 0) log(y_ex) else (y_ex^l - 1) / l
  fit <- arima(z, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
  fit$loglik + (l - 1) * sum(log(y_ex), na.rm = TRUE)
})
lams[which.max(ll_ex)] # best lambda without the absence blocks


# ---- Figure 2 ----
dir.create(here("R_figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
png(here("R_figures", "01d_boxcox_profile.png"), width = 7, height = 4, units = "in", res = 140)
plot(lams, ll - max(ll), type = "b", ylim = range(c(ll - max(ll), ll_ex - max(ll_ex))),
     xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "log-likelihood minus its maximum")
lines(lams, ll_ex - max(ll_ex), type = "b", col = "red")
abline(h = -qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, lty = 2)   # points above this line are in the 95% CI
legend("bottomleft", c("All observed days", "Absence blocks removed"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
dev.off()

# ---- Table 2 ----
# CHECK RESIDUAL DIAGNOSTICS (innovations from the regression with AR(1) errors)
skew <- function(e) { e <- e[!is.na(e)]; mean((e - mean(e))^3) / sd(e)^3 }
kurt <- function(e) { e <- e[!is.na(e)]; mean((e - mean(e))^4) / sd(e)^4 }
fit_scale <- function(l) {
  z <- if (l == 0) log(d$kwh) else (d$kwh^l - 1) / l   # Box-Cox transform (l = 0 is log)
  arima(z, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X)
}
lam_hat <- lams[which.max(ll)]                         # Box-Cox best lambda (0.4)
mon <- format(d$date, "%m")
scales <- c(0, lam_hat, 0.5, 1) # transformations to consider
names(scales) <- c("Log (λ = 0)",
                   paste0("Box-Cox best (λ = ", lam_hat, ")"),
                   "Square root (λ = 0.5)",
                   "kWh, no transform (λ = 1)")

  s <- tapply(e[!core], mon[!core], sd, na.rm = TRUE)   # monthly SD, absence-block days excluded
  c(Skew = skew(e), Kurtosis = kurt(e), "Max/min monthly SD" = max(s) / min(s))
}))

             caption = paste("Table 2. Innovations from the regression with AR(1) errors",
                             "(trend + two harmonics + day of week) on each scale.",
                             "Normal errors have skew 0 and kurtosis 3."))
# A Box–Cox profile likelihood allowing AR(1) errors favors λ ≈ 0.4 with or without the absence blocks. The square-root scale (λ = 0.5) gives nearly symmetric innovations (skew −0.07 vs 0.43), lighter tails, and more even monthly spread (SD ratio 1.96 vs 2.37), so we will model √kWh and report results in kWh through Monte Carlo transformation of posterior draws.

# Uses from earlier chunks: d (full calendar), X (design matrix), core (absence-block days), here()

skew_adj <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  xc <- x - mean(x)
  m2 <- sum(xc^2) / n
  m3 <- sum(xc^3) / n
  (m3 / m2^1.5) * sqrt(n * (n - 1)) / (n - 2)
}

# Uses from earlier chunks: d, core, MONTHS, ols(), harmonic_cols(), dow_dummies(), here()

# helpers used only by this figure (unchanged from the script)
# autocorrelation at calendar lags, so gaps from missing days are respected
acf_calendar <- function(resid, t, nlags) {
  tt <- as.integer(round(t))
  pos <- integer(max(tt))
  pos[tt] <- seq_along(tt)
  out <- numeric(nlags)
  for (k in seq_len(nlags)) {
    prev <- tt - k
    ok <- prev >= 1L & prev <= length(pos)
    j <- integer(length(tt))
    j[ok] <- pos[prev[ok]]
    ok <- ok & j > 0L
    a <- resid[ok]
    b <- resid[j[ok]]
    a <- a - mean(a)
    b <- b - mean(b)
    out[k] <- sum(a * b) / sqrt(sum(a * a) * sum(b * b))
  }
  out
}

# partial autocorrelation from the ACF via Yule-Walker
pacf_yw <- function(rho) {
  pac <- numeric(length(rho))
  for (k in seq_along(rho)) {
    r <- rho[seq_len(k)]
    if (k == 1) {
      pac[k] <- r[1]
      next
    }
    R <- matrix(0, k, k)
    for (i in seq_len(k)) for (j in seq_len(k)) {
      lag <- abs(i - j)
      R[i, j] <- if (lag == 0) 1 else rho[lag]
    }
    phi <- tryCatch(solve(R, r), error = function(e) qr.solve(R, r))
    pac[k] <- phi[k]
  }
  pac
}

bic_ar <- function(z, n) sapply(1:5, function(p) {
  fit <- arima(z, order = c(p, 0, 0), xreg = X)
  -2 * fit$loglik + log(n) * (length(fit$coef) + 1)
})

# 2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Bayesian Model

## 2.1 General Patterns

```{r fig1, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 1. (a) Daily consumption with missing days marked in red; (b) daily data coverage with the 95% threshold; (c) annual shape by year with one- and two-harmonic fits; (d) weekdays versus weekends; (e) consumption by day of week."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "01d_overview.png"))
```

In the above panel, we look at daily household energy consumption throughout the whole time series, as well as its seasonal and weekly variation. As we can see in Figure 1a, daily household energy consumption has a clear yearly wave, but no real overall drift, pointing to negligible long-run changes but substantial seasonal variation. Looking at the seasonal variation, our data is an intuitive U-shape, higher electricity consumption in the winter months and lower electricity consumption in the summer months, with a relatively smooth shape- both harmonics seem to fit the overall pattern. Lastly, looking at the weekly variation, we can see that there are recurring differences across the seven days of the week, especially with Saturday and Sunday having slightly higher means and larger Interquartile ranges (IQRs) than weekdays. Overall, weekends are higher than weekdays (Figure 1d), but the weekdays also differ (Figure 1e). Therefore, we use day-of-week effects and recover the weekend as a contrast of the day-of-week coefficients (Section 5).

## 2.2 Response Variable 

```{r tab1}
tab1_kbl
```

We then look at whether transforming $Y_d$ improves the residual behavior. Since the data form a time series, we check the independence of errors (Table 1). On every scale, the Ordinary Least Squares residuals are strongly auto-correlated, so we use a Box–Cox profile likelihood under a regression with AR(1) errors (Box & Cox, 1964; Ansley et al., 1977).

```{r fig-boxcox, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "Figure 2. Box–Cox profile log-likelihood under a regression with AR(1) errors (trend + two harmonics + day of week), with all observed days (black) and with absence-block days removed (red). Each curve is shifted so its maximum is 0; values of λ above the dashed line lie inside the 95% confidence interval."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "01d_boxcox_profile.png"))
```

```{r tab2}
tab2_kbl
```

Lower $\lambda$ evens out the monthly spread but pushes skew negative (Table 2): log over-corrects (skew −0.44, kurtosis 4.91). The square root balances the two, with nearly symmetric innovations (skew −0.07), the lowest kurtosis, and an SD ratio below 2, and is practically equivalent to the Box–Cox optimum ($\hat{\lambda} = 0.4$). Therefore, we will perform a square root transformation of our response variable Y ($\sqrt{Y}=\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$).

We model each day’s error with two parts: a carried-over part and a new surprise, the innovation. Because kurtosis stays above 3 on every scale, the innovation follows a t-distribution, making it usually small while allowing occasional extremely high- or low-consumption days.

The profile likelihood peaks at $\hat\lambda \approx 0.4$ both with and without the absence-block days (Figure 2), so the transformation is not driven by the vacations.

```{r fig3, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 3. Residual checks on the square-root scale, using innovations from the regression with AR(1) errors (trend + two harmonics + day of week): (a) over time, with absence-block days in red; (b) against one-step fitted values; (c) normal Q-Q plot."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "01d_residual_checks_sqrt.png"))
```

The smoothed residuals stay close to zero, so the regression with AR(1) errors captures the main structure of the data (Figure 3a). There are still some small uncaptured wiggles, so the two harmonics may not capture the seasonal effects perfectly. Three of the red absence blocks are in the summer, so these are likely when the household is away on vacation.

Even after accounting for the AR(1) carry-over, the residuals within the absence blocks stay negative for many consecutive days, while elsewhere the residuals show no long same-sign runs. This suggests AR(1) captures the ordinary day-to-day dependence. The t errors are intended to absorb isolated extreme days, such as the shorter grey dips. The sustained absence blocks are departures that neither AR(1) nor the t errors is designed to capture fully, and we will revisit them after model-fitting. On the square-root scale, the residuals show no clear funnel shape against the fitted values (Figure 3b), so heteroscedasticity is not a major concern. The smoothed curve bends slightly downward at both ends, where there are few points. At the low end this is partly a floor effect from absence days rather than a misfit of the mean. Seasonal coverage of the predictive intervals will be checked in Section 6 to confirm that any remaining heteroskedasticity is not a limitation of our model. Lastly, the normal Q-Q plot shows symmetric residuals (skew −0.07) with heavy tails at both ends, which is supported by Table 2 and is exactly what the t errors are aimed at.
```{r tab3}
tab3_kbl
```
Missing days are not clustered around absence periods (Table 3: 1.2% of days in or within three days of an absence block are missing, versus 1.6% elsewhere), so they appear to come from recording outages rather than from the meter being switched off before a vacation. This is consistent with missingness at random, and the missing days make up only 1.6% of the calendar. Since MAR cannot be verified from the observed data, it remains an assumption.

## 2.3 Temporal Dependence

```{r fig4, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 4. (a) Residual ACF and (b) residual PACF on the square-root scale, for all observed days (bars) and with absence blocks removed (red); (c) residual SD by month."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "01d_residual_sqrt.png"))
```

```{r tab-dependence}
tab4_kbl
```

```{r bic-table}
bic_tab
```

After accounting for the intercept, trend, seasonality, and day-of-week effects, the residuals on the square-root scale remain correlated over time (Figure 4a, Table 4). The lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.47, but it decays much slower than the AR(1) prediction. The absence blocks explain part of this: they are 4.0% of observed days but 19.1% of the residual sum of squares, and removing them lowers the lag-1 autocorrelation to 0.35. The partial autocorrelations show that this extra memory lasts a few days rather than following a weekly cycle. Lags 2–4 still exceed the ±0.05 bounds. Further, by BIC AR(4) errors fit best both with and without the absence blocks, So the AR order should be chosen by model comparison rather than fixed from the EDA. For now, we fit AR(1) errors.

# !Do we really need this part and figure 4c??? NO (keep figure 4 for now in case it is needed later)

Residual spread is highest in February and lowest in September (Figure 4c). August is high only because of the absence blocks and drops to typical levels without them.

Panel (c) uses OLS residuals, which still contain the day-to-day carry-over. With blocks removed, its February/September ratio is about 2.3 (0.93/0.40 read off the plot), while Table 2’s ratio of 1.96 uses the AR(1) innovations, the errors the model actually assumes. A reader comparing the two might think you contradicted yourself. If you keep the panel, add a clause like “(these OLS residuals include the carried-over part, so their spread is larger than that of the innovations in Table 2)”. Dropping the panel avoids the issue, and that’s the safest choice here since it also gets rid of the need for adding extra commentary.

One more point to be aware of: the PACF also has a negative spike at lag 8 (about −0.11 in both versions), beyond the bounds. It’s isolated and doesn’t change the conclusion, but someone reading the figure closely might ask about it. If we want to cover it, add “an isolated negative value at lag 8 aside”.


## 2.4 Implications for Model

Based on the previous sections, we formulate our Bayesian model for the square-root of daily consumption. It accounts for a long-term linear trend (even if the evidence for it is negligible), seasonality, day-of-week effects, temporal dependency, and the absence periods:

$$\begin{align}
z_{t} &= x_{t}^{T}\beta+\varepsilon_{t}\\
\hspace{0.5cm}x_{t}^{T}\beta &= \beta_{0}+\beta_{1}\frac{t-\bar{t}}{365}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\left[a_{j}\sin\frac{2\pi jt}{365}+b_{j}\cos\frac{2\pi jt}{365}\right]+\sum_{k=2}^{7}\delta_{k}1\left\{\text{dow}_{t} =k\right\} \hspace{0.5cm} \\
\varepsilon_{t}&=\sum_{l=1}^{p}\phi_{l}\varepsilon_{t-l}+\eta_{t},\hspace{0.5cm}\eta_{t}\sim t_{\nu}(0,\sigma^{2})
\end{align}$$

$z_{t}$ is $\sqrt{Y_t}$, $\beta_{0}$ is the intercept, $\beta_{1}$ is the long-run linear trend, centered at the middle of our observations. $a_{j},b_{j}$ are the coefficients for the harmonic trends, and $\delta_{k}$ are the day-of-week effects (with the base being Monday). Additionally, $\sum_{l=1}^{p}\phi_{l}\varepsilon_{t-l}$ is the autocorrelated error and $\varepsilon_{t}$ is the error that isn't explained by autocorrelation, following a t-distribution to account for the absence periods.

Our main model uses J=2 harmonics and AR(1) (p=1), and J=1 and AR(2)-AR(4) will be compared in Section 5.

We will use Bayesian data augmentation using Gibbs sampling to handle the missing days that are MAR (Section 2.2) so that imputation uncertainty propagates into all posterior summaries and forecasts.

#      col = col_red, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c(col_nav, col_teal), cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(sprintf("intercept, SD %g", TAU_INT), sprintf("other coefficients, SD %g", TAU_OTH)))

# (b) innovation scale: folded t_3 with scale A, f(s) = 2 * dt(s/A, 3) / A for s > 0
xs <- seq(0.01, 10, length.out = 600)
ds <- 2 * dt(xs / A_SIGMA, df = 3) / A_SIGMA
plot(xs, ds, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_nav,
     xlab = "innovation scale (sqrt kWh)", ylab = "prior density", main = "(b) Innovation scale")
abline(v = sd_p, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5, col = col_red)
text(sd_p + 0.2, 0.9 * max(ds), sprintf("SD of daily sqrt kWh = %.2f", sd_p), col = col_red, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
text(6.5, 0.5 * max(ds), sprintf("half-t, 3 df\nscale %g", A_SIGMA), col = col_nav, cex = 0.75)

# (c) AR(1) coefficient: uniform on the stationary interval
plot(NA, xlim = c(-1.45, 1.45), ylim = c(0, 0.75), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = expression("autoregressive coefficient" ~ phi), ylab = "prior density",
     main = "(c) AR(1) coefficient")
rect(-1.45, 0, -1, 0.75, col = "#f6e6e4", border = NA)
rect(1, 0, 1.45, 0.75, col = "#f6e6e4", border = NA)
rect(-1, 0, 1, 0.5, col = adjustcolor(col_nav, 0.18), border = col_nav, lwd = 2)
text(0, 0.58, "stationary: shocks fade", col = col_nav, cex = 0.75)
text(-1.22, 0.62, "excluded", col = col_red, cex = 0.65, srt = 90)
text(1.22, 0.62, "excluded", col = col_red, cex = 0.65, srt = 90)
axis(1, at = c(-1, 0, 1))

# (d) degrees of freedom: nu - 2 ~ Exp(mean 10)
nu_grid <- seq(2.02, 48, length.out = 500)
dn <- dexp(nu_grid - 2, rate = 0.1)
plot(nu_grid, dn, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_nav,
     xlab = expression("degrees of freedom" ~ nu), ylab = "prior density", main = "(d) Tail weight")
abline(v = 2, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5, col = col_red)
abline(v = 12, lty = 3, lwd = 1.5, col = col_gold)
text(3.1, 0.085, expression(nu == 2), col = col_red, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
text(13.2, 0.07, "prior mean of nu = 12", col = col_gold, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
text(32, 0.04, "nearly\nGaussian", col = col_nav, cex = 0.75)
dev.off()
```

# 3. Prior Distributions

```{r tab-priors}
tab_priors_kbl
```

```{r fig-priors, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 5. Prior densities on the square-root scale: (a) regression coefficients, with the largest gap between monthly mean square-root consumption for reference; (b) innovation scale, with the standard deviation of daily square-root consumption; (c) AR(1) coefficient, uniform on the stationary region; (d) degrees of freedom."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "03_prior_densities.png"))
```
This dataset was previously been used mainly to benchmark machine-learning forecasters at minute or hourly resolution (e.g., Kim & Cho, 2019), including Bayesian neural networks for uncertainty estimation (Zaman et al., 2022). We instead fit an interpretable Bayesian regression to daily totals, with seasonal, weekly, autoregressive and heavy-tailed components. There are no published estimates of these model parameters for a comparable household, so we utilized weakly informative priors to allow our data to be the primary thing informing our posterior distributions (Table 5, Figure 5). 

The priors are centered at zero and are not derived from the data; we compare them with summaries of the data only to confirm that they are wide relative to plausible values. With our large sample size (over 1,000 training days), we expect posterior estimates to be insensitive to this choice, but the tail parameter $\nu$, which the data inform least, may not be. Therefore, Section 6 refits the model with the coefficient prior standard deviations halved and doubled, and with the prior on $\nu$ shifted toward heavier and toward lighter tails.

First, the intercept $\beta_0$ has a normal prior, which is continuous, symmetric, and allows any real value. Its standard deviation of 20 $\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$ places 95% of the prior within ±40 $\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$ (up to 40² = 1,600 kWh/day), far above the current average for a Sceaux household (about 9.6 kWh per day; GridLabs, n.d.), this household’s highest observed day (about 80 kWh), and even the physical maximum of a residential connection (864 kWh/day; EDF, Tarif Bleu), so the prior does not constrain the intercept. Our mean is 0 not because we believe the baseline level is zero, but because with that standard deviation, it is nonrestrictive (Figure 5a).  

Second, our other regression coefficients $\beta_1, a_j, b_j, \delta_k$ also have normal priors centered at 0 for similar reasons: it is continuous, symmetric, lets the data choose the direction of each effect, and makes extremely large effects less plausible. Their standard deviation of 5 √kWh is about twice the largest contrast in the data (Figure 5a).

Third, the innovation scale $\sigma$ has a half-$t$ prior with 3 degrees of freedom and scale 2 √kWh (Gelman, 2006). It keeps $\sigma$ positive and its heavy tails allows scales well above the standard deviation of daily √kWh, 1.01 (Figure 5b). 

Fourth, the autoregressive coefficients have a uniform prior on the stationary region: $(-1, 1)$ for AR(1), and the corresponding stationary region for the higher-order models compared in Section 5. Within that region every value is equally likely, and shocks fade over time, so long-horizon forecasts stay bounded (Figure 5c).

Fifth, for our degrees of freedom $\nu$, we choose an exponential prior with mean 10 for $\nu-2$, for similar reasons of why we chose the half-t distribution. We want to restrict the values to values greater than 2 (the t distribution only has finite variance when the degrees of freedom are greater than 2), and we're trying to accommodate heavy-tailed innovations [(the exponential distribution allows us to do this while also assigning less probability to extremely large values. The degrees of freedom determine how heavy the innovation distribution's tails are: smaller values produce heavier tails, while larger values produce increasingly Gaussian-like distributions. The Exponential prior allows us to accommodate heavy-tailed innovations by assigning substantial prior density to values of $\nu$ near 2, while progressively reducing the density assigned to extremely large values of $\nu$. **Shorter alternative of this paragraph:** Fifth, an exponential prior with mean 10 on $\nu - 2$ keeps $\nu$ above 2, so the innovation variance is finite. It puts substantial weight on small values (heavy tails) and less on very large ones (nearly Gaussian tails), so the data decide how heavy the tails are (Figure 5d).

#! prior for latent weights ???

The 23 missing days need no separate prior: their distribution is implied by the regression and the autoregressive process, and they are sampled within the Gibbs sampler.

Together, these choices regularize the parameters without imposing a direction or size on the household's demand patterns in advance.

# 4. Posterior Computation and Diagnostics

```{r post-run, include = FALSE}
# Posterior for sections 4 and 5. src/06_fit_sqrt.R runs the MCMC (about 12 minutes) and
# src/07_sqrt_results.R turns the draws into the tables, figures and numbers used below.
# They run only when results/06_sqrt/summary.rds is missing; delete it to redo the summaries.
post_dir <- here("results", "06_sqrt")
fit_files <- file.path(post_dir, paste0(c("main", "J1", "ar2", "kwh", "holdout", "holdout_ar2"), ".rds"))
if (!file.exists(file.path(post_dir, "summary.rds"))) {
  if (!all(file.exists(fit_files))) system2("Rscript", shQuote(here("src", "06_fit_sqrt.R")))
  system2("Rscript", shQuote(here("src", "07_sqrt_results.R")))
}
```

The posterior has no closed form, so we sample it with a Gibbs sampler written for this model (`src/model.R`), following Chib (1993) for the autoregressive errors and Geweke (1993) for the $t$ errors. Three augmentations make most full conditionals standard: each $t$ error is a normal error with a latent weight, $\eta_t \mid \lambda_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2/\lambda_t)$ with $\lambda_t \sim \text{Gamma}(\nu/2, \nu/2)$; the half-$t$ prior on $\sigma$ is an inverse-gamma mixture; and the 23 missing days are unknowns. Each iteration draws $\beta$ from a multivariate normal, $\sigma^2$ from an inverse gamma, each $\lambda_t$ from a gamma, and each missing day from a normal. $\phi$ and $\nu$ have no standard full conditional, so they take random-walk Metropolis steps, rejecting non-stationary $\phi$. Step sizes are tuned during burn-in and then frozen; afterwards, 29% of $\phi$ and 30% of $\nu$ proposals are accepted.

We ran four chains of 40,000 iterations from dispersed starting values of $\sigma$, $\phi$, $\nu$, and the missing days, discarded the first 10,000, and kept every fifth draw, leaving 24,000 draws. Table 5 reports the rank-normalized split-$\hat{R}$ and the bulk and tail effective sample sizes (ESS) of Vehtari et al. (2021). The worst $\hat{R}$ is 1.006 and the smallest ESS is 677, against targets of 1.01 and 400, so Monte Carlo error is below 4% of every posterior standard deviation. $\nu$ mixes slowest because the data inform it only through the latent weights. In Figure 6, all four chains leave their starting values within a few hundred iterations and then overlap.

We trust these draws because chains started far apart agree, every diagnostic clears its target, and on data simulated from the model the sampler's 95% intervals covered 14 of 15 true parameter values (`src/02_validate_sampler.R`). The comparison and holdout fits in Section 5 meet the same targets.

```{r table5, echo = FALSE}
tab5 <- read.csv(file.path(post_dir, "table_convergence.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
names(tab5)[names(tab5) == "Worst R-hat"] <- "Worst $\\hat{R}$"
knitr::kable(
  tab5, escape = FALSE, align = "llcrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "Table 5. Sampler steps and convergence diagnostics for the final model (four chains, 24,000 kept draws).",
    "$\\hat{R}$ is the larger of the bulk and folded rank-normalized split-$\\hat{R}$.",
    "Targets: $\\hat{R} < 1.01$ and ESS above 400."
  )
)
```

```{r fig6, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 6. Trace plots for the trend, innovation scale, autoregressive coefficient, and degrees of freedom, including the discarded burn-in (shaded), with each chain's density of kept draws on the right."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "06_trace.png"))
```

# 5. Posterior Results and Interpretation

We transform each posterior draw from $\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$ to kWh and summarize the *typical day*, $(x_t^\top\beta)^2$, which is the median daily consumption given the parameters because the error is symmetric on the square-root scale (Table 6).

```{r table6, echo = FALSE}
tab6 <- read.csv(file.path(post_dir, "table_posterior.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  tab6, escape = FALSE, align = "llr",
  caption = paste(
    "Table 6. Posterior means and 95% credible intervals (CrI). kWh quantities refer to the typical day",
    "at the record midpoint, averaged over the week or the year as appropriate."
  )
)
```

**Variation and trend (Q1, Q2).** A typical day uses 25.8 kWh [95% CrI 25.2, 26.4]; variation around that level is seasonal, weekly, and day-to-day, not a drift. The annual mean changes by −0.20 kWh per year [−0.77, 0.37], or −0.8% [−3.0, 1.4]. A decline has posterior probability 0.76, but the interval includes zero, so there is no clear long-term increase or decrease.

**Annual cycle (Q3).** Typical use peaks at 35.1 kWh [33.4, 36.8] in mid-December and falls to 15.9 kWh [14.8, 17.0] in early August, a swing of 19.2 kWh (Figure 7a). The second harmonic is an important improvement: it moves the curve by up to 3.2 kWh [2.2, 4.3], flattening late winter and deepening the summer trough, and raises WAIC's expected log predictive density by 15.6 (SE 6.1).

**Weekly pattern (Q4).** Weekends use 4.4 kWh [3.5, 5.3] more than weekdays in every posterior draw. Weekdays also differ: Thursday is lowest, 2.7 kWh [1.9, 3.5] below the weekly mean (Figure 7b).

```{r fig7, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 7. (a) Posterior typical-day consumption over the year with 95% credible bands, for the final two-harmonic model and the one-harmonic model; dots are observed monthly medians. (b) Day-of-week effects relative to the weekly mean, with 95% credible intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "07_season_week.png"))
```

**Forecasting (Q5).** We refit through November 2009 and forecast the final year (Figure 8). The mean 95% interval is 27.5 kWh wide one day ahead and 30–31 kWh from day three onward, matching the limit $1/\sqrt{1-\phi^2} = 1.13$ implied by $\phi = 0.47$ [0.42, 0.52]. After a few days, recent consumption stops being informative and forecasts reduce to the seasonal and weekly pattern. The intervals are calibrated (97.6% and 53% coverage at the 95% and 50% levels) but wide: the 12-month forecast misses by 5.2 kWh per day on average, a fifth of typical use.

```{r fig8, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 8. Forecasting the held-out final year from a fit through 30 November 2009. (a) Twelve-month predictive median with 50% and 95% intervals against actual consumption; (b) mean 95% interval width and (c) empirical coverage by horizon, over 113 rolling forecast origins."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "08_forecast.png"))
```

**Unexplained periods (Q6).** Single days are flagged about as often as chance predicts: 30 of 1,408 one-step-ahead predictive p-values fall below 0.01 or above 0.99, against 28 expected. The $t$ errors ($\nu = 8.4$ [5.8, 12.4]) give 20 isolated extreme days less than half weight, but not the absence blocks, whose low level the AR(1) term carries forward. Sustained periods are not explained: comparing each 14-day mean with its posterior predictive distribution flags 10 episodes (Figure 9). Eight are low, including all three August absences, when use fell to 56–67% of a typical day; two are high, both in the first winter. Calendar terms cannot anticipate these behavioral episodes.

```{r fig9, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 9. Observed consumption against the model's typical day. Shading marks 14-day periods whose mean falls outside the central 98% of its posterior predictive distribution; circles mark days the t likelihood gives less than half weight."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("R_figures", "09_anomalies.png"))
```

# 6. Sensitivity Analysis and Model Checking


**Prior sensitivity.** We refit the final model four times, changing one prior at a time: the coefficient prior standard deviations halved (intercept 10, others 2.5 $\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$) or doubled (40 and 10), and the prior mean of $\nu - 2$ lowered from 10 to 3 (heavier tails) or raised to 30 (nearly Gaussian tails). No conclusion changes (Table 8). Every kWh summary moves by at most 0.02 posterior standard deviations, $P(\text{decline})$ stays at 0.75–0.76, and WAIC's elpd changes by at most 0.2. Even $\nu$ stays between 7.8 and 8.6 while its prior mean ranges from 5 to 32, so the evidence for heavy tails comes from the data.

**Modelling assumptions.** On the same 1,399 likelihood terms, dropping the second harmonic lowers WAIC's elpd by 15.6 (SE 6.1), and modelling raw kWh lowers it by 53.1 (SE 8.6). AR(2) errors raise it by 15.5 (SE 7.4) but forecast the held-out year slightly worse (log score −0.004 per forecast, SE 0.002), so we keep AR(1).

**Posterior predictive checks.** Across 2,000 series simulated from the posterior, the model reproduces day-to-day persistence, skewness, the highest day and the number of low days (Table 9, Figure 11). The winter-to-summer spread ratio is borderline ($p = 0.065$): the square-root scale removes most, not all, of the extra winter variability. The observed longest run below 12 kWh, 25 days, is never replicated (95% interval 3–9 days), so the model cannot generate the absence blocks found under Q6.

**Calibration by season.** Held-out 95% intervals cover 97.3–97.9% of days in every season, widening from 25.5 kWh in summer to 34.9 kWh in winter, so the winter variability noted in Section 2.2 does not miscalibrate them (Table 10). The 50% intervals are less even (44–64%).

The answers to Q1–Q5 are robust to the priors and to these modelling choices; the only failure is the sustained absences already reported under Q6.

# 7. Alternative Analysis, Comparison, and Bayesian Justification

```{r freq-run, include = FALSE}
# Section 7. src/08_frequentist.R fits the final model by maximum likelihood (about 5 seconds)
# and writes Table 7 and Figure 10. It runs only when results/08_freq/summary.rds is missing.
freq_dir <- here("results", "08_freq")
if (!file.exists(file.path(freq_dir, "summary.rds"))) system2("Rscript", shQuote(here("src", "08_frequentist.R")))
```

**Frequentist analysis.** We refit the final model (the same $\sqrt{\text{kWh}}$ mean structure and AR(1) $t$ errors) by maximum likelihood, with no priors. The likelihood conditions on the first day of each observed run, so the 23 missing days drop out rather than being imputed, leaving 1,408 terms. Standard errors come from the observed information. Typical-day kWh quantities are nonlinear in $\beta$, so their confidence intervals come from simulating the estimator's asymptotic normal distribution (Krinsky and Robb, 1986). Forecasts plug the training-period estimates into the AR(1) recursion and are scored on the same 113 rolling origins as Section 5.

**Estimates and uncertainty.** Every typical-day estimate agrees with its posterior mean to within 0.4 kWh, and their interval widths differ by under 2% (Table 7, Figure 10a). With 1,408 likelihood terms, the weakly informative priors carry almost no weight. The largest difference is the tail weight, $\hat\nu = 7.7$ against a posterior mean of 8.4, because the posterior of $\nu$ is right-skewed and its prior mean is 12.

**Interpretation.** The conclusions match; only the wording differs. For the trend, the frequentist analysis cannot reject zero ($p = 0.55$), while the Bayesian analysis gives a decline probability 0.76. That is close to one minus the one-sided $p$-value (0.72), as expected under weak priors, but only the Bayesian number is a probability about this household's trend. Both keep the second harmonic: the likelihood-ratio test gives $\chi^2_2 = 34.3$ ($p < 0.001$), and AIC improves by 30.3, close to the WAIC gain of 15.6 expressed on the same deviance scale (31.2).

**Predictions.** Plug-in intervals treat the estimates as known, so they are 1.6% narrower one day ahead and 2.5% narrower from day three onward (Figure 10b). Their 95% coverage is 97.2%, against 97.6% (Figure 10c), and both 12-month forecasts miss by 5.2 kWh per day on average. Drawing the parameters from the estimator's sampling distribution closes most of the width gap, so parameter uncertainty is a small part of forecast uncertainty here.

**Why Bayesian?** For this household, the Bayesian analysis adds little to the estimates or forecasts: four years of daily data give both methods the same answers to all six questions. Its advantages are interpretation and bookkeeping. Every kWh summary, including peak dates and the 14-day anomaly check, comes from transforming posterior draws, with no delta method or asymptotic approximation. Parameter uncertainty, the 23 missing days and the latent $t$ weights all reach the forecasts without extra steps. A question like "how likely is a decline?" gets a direct answer. The cost is 12 minutes of MCMC and convergence checking, against 5 seconds of optimization. With less data, such as a newly metered household, the priors and full predictive distribution would matter more.

  )
